Reapers
REE-perz
noun (plural)
From reap, the Saxon ripan, to cut grain, akin to ripe; hence those who cut down the standing corn at harvest. It renders the Hebrew qatsar in the participle and the Greek theristes.

Biblical Definition

Reapers are the labourers who cut the standing corn and bind it, working under an overseer and followed by the gleaners who gather what falls. Scripture gives us one memorable company of them: Boaz’s men in the barley fields of Bethlehem. Ruth the Moabitess “gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech” (Rut 2:3) — her hap, which is providence speaking in the language of ordinary days. Boaz comes from Bethlehem and greets his workmen, “The LORD be with you,” and they answer, “The LORD bless thee” (Rut 2:4): the field is a place of covenant courtesy, not mere labour. He charges the young men not to touch her, bids her drink of their vessels, and commands them to let handfuls fall on purpose. So the kinsman-redeemer is first met among his reapers, providing for a widow in the ordinary channels of harvest and gleaning-law, before he ever stands at the gate to redeem her. Christ takes the same picture into eternity. Expounding the tares, He says the harvest is the end of the world, “and the reapers are the angels” (Mat 13:39), sent to gather the tares in bundles to burn and the wheat into the barn (Mat 13:30). And James warns those who defraud reapers of their hire that the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth (Jas 5:4). The men in the field foreshadow the angels at the end; the Lord of the harvest pays and reckons both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Those who cut down the standing corn at harvest; Boaz’s men among whom Ruth gleaned, and Christ’s figure for the angels at the end of the world.

REAPER, n. [From reap, Saxon ripan, to cut grain.] One that cuts grain with a sickle; a harvest labourer.

In Scripture, the workmen of the field, followed by gleaners according to the law of Lev 19:9.

The reapers of Boaz among whom Ruth gathered (Rut 2:3–9).

Their hire was due the same day, and fraud in withholding it cries to God (Jas 5:4; Deu 24:15).

Figuratively, the angels sent forth at the end of the world (Mat 13:39).

Key Scripture

Rut 2:3 — "And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech."

Rut 2:4 — "And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee."

Mat 13:39 — "The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels."

Jas 5:4 — "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

Modern Corruption

The book of Ruth is read as a romance and the reapers as scenery, while the final harvest of Mat 13 is softened until the reapers gather nobody into the fire.

expand to see more

Two flattenings are common. The first turns Ruth into a love story with a religious setting, so that Boaz is an admirable man rather than the kinsman-redeemer whose right to redeem must be established at the gate, and the field becomes a picturesque backdrop rather than the working of God’s gleaning-law, which fed the widow and the stranger without alms and without shame. The second empties Mat 13:39. The Lord’s own interpretation of the tares is as plain as language can be: the harvest is the end of the world, the reapers are angels, the tares are bound in bundles and burned, and there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Annihilationist and universalist readings must dispose of that sentence, and no reading which does so has honoured the One who spoke it. The reapers are sent by the Son of man, and their commission includes a fire.

Recover the two harvests together, for they are one lesson. Boaz in the barley field is Christ in the world — the redeemer who greets his labourers with the LORD be with you, who orders handfuls to fall on purpose for a foreign widow with no claim, and who at last takes her to himself by right of kinship and price paid. The angels at the end are the same Lord’s servants completing the same work: gathering His wheat into the barn. And between them stands James’s warning to every employer — pay the reaper his hire, and pay it today, because the Lord of sabaoth hears what the labourer cannot say to your face.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Harvest labourers; Boaz’s men behind whom Ruth gleaned, and the angels the Son of man sends at the end of the world.

expand to see more

Reaper — from reap, Saxon ripan, to cut grain; akin to ripe.

Hebrew qotserim, the cutters (Rut 2:3–9); Greek theristai (Mat 13:39).

The reapers go first, the gleaners follow — the law’s provision for widow and stranger (Lev 19:9).

Boaz sets a servant over the reapers and charges them for Ruth’s protection (Rut 2:5, 9).

Mat 13:30, 39 — tares bound in bundles, wheat into the barn, by angelic hands.

Usage

"Ruth’s “hap” is the Bible’s way of showing providence dressed as coincidence."

"Boaz among his reapers is the kinsman-redeemer before he is ever called that at the gate."

"Mat 13:39 identifies the reapers definitively: the angels, at the end of the world."
